verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Chennai electronics component and device makers with contracted order books and tight working-capital control; avoid thin-margin assemblers riding the memory-price revenue illusion.
title: Chennai Electronics Manufacturing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Chennai electronics is a conversion business: imported components in, assembled devices out, cash earned on the spread between component cost and selling price.** OMRON's new 24,000 sq m plant near Chennai with five production lines making blood pressure monitors is the template — imported sub-assemblies, local labour, quality control transferred from Japan and Vietnam [1]. Value sits in the customer relationship and the quality certification, not the building. **Capex is lumpy and front-loaded; working capital is the real risk.** Component inventory and receivables against a handful of large buyers decide whether a good year produces cash or just revenue.

## What has changed now
**National electronics output is running hot — IIP NIC 26 at +19.3% YoY and +13.6% Apr-to-date, exports +44.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D] — but Tamil Nadu's GST collections fell 3.2% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D].** That 9.3 pp gap is a local demand and compliance signal, so when a proposal lands, check the borrower's own GST filings against the state trend; if a Chennai assembler shows flat GST turnover while claiming 30% growth, ask for the buyer-wise sales register. **Peer results show revenue growth that is partly price, not volume.** Dixon's Q2 FY27 revenue rose 47% to Rs 21,794 crore while margins compressed and working capital burden rose [6][7], and NDTV Profit reports the lift comes from memory chip prices with smartphone volumes broadly unchanged [4]. So when a proposal lands, separate price-led revenue from unit growth; if the borrower's volumes are flat, ask why it needs more working capital.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue tier-2 component and sub-assembly suppliers to the new Chennai anchor plants, and medical-device and IT-hardware makers with domestic order books.** OMRON targets about 3 million units annually by 2028 with potential for about 3.5 million on three shifts, and plans to supply Europe from Chennai [1] — that creates local sourcing demand. Dixon's INR 15,000–20,000 crore IT-hardware target for laptops, tablets and desktops [5] signals where contract demand sits. **Avoid pure assemblers with single-customer concentration and no design or tooling content**; they carry the memory-price swing and pass none of it through.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the order book, not the P&L.** Take monthly stock-and-debtor statements, a charge on receivables from named buyers, and a covenant capping inventory days. Take every month: GST returns, buyer-wise sales, inventory ageing and a component price index note. **Where the borrower's margin depends on a component price the customer has not yet accepted, ask for the price-pass-through clause in writing.** Rating reports on this segment are undated in our file [8][9][10], so treat them as background only.

## Early-warning signs
- **GST turnover falling faster than the Tamil Nadu state trend [D] (monthly) -> freeze new limits and re-verify buyer orders.**
- **Inventory days rising while revenue grows on price alone [4] (monthly) -> ask for the component price contract and cut limit.**
- **Single buyer above 50% of receivables (quarterly) -> require diversification plan before renewal.**
- **Margin compression with revenue growth, as at Dixon [6] (quarterly) -> reprice or exit at renewal.**
